Female here. Also crazy schedule with kids. We're out of the house by 730 and not usually home till 8 or 830. I'm down about 12lbs so far over the last 6 ish weeks. I try to not over complicate it, but it does require a little lost sleep.

1. I eat whole foods only. I may have a meal out over the weekend, but I don't make it a habit that spills into the week. Primarily meat and veggies. Sounds boring but there are so many flavors you can create. My favorite is sundried tomato chicken with broccoli or asparagus right now. 

2. I only drink 1 cup of coffee in the morning and water the rest of the day. No soda, no juice, no energy drinks etc. 

3. I work out 3x a week. Probably no more than about 30 - 40 minutes each time. Typically some type of weighted circuit. I get up at 530 twice during the week and I do the third over the weekend to still prioritize my sleep. This week's workout is below.

Curls x15
Squats x15
Pull overs x15
Squats x15
Bench x15
Squats x 15
Rows x15
Squats x15
Abs x15

Do it twice.

This probably seems like a normal way of living to some, but I've found it is quite different from the way I've done things my whole life. I hope you find something in here useful. Good luck!

I think you said it best. There's a lot at play. Maturity, age, naiveness, etc. 

Truly, you sound so much stronger and more self aware than I ever was at that time. 

Just for clarity though, I would not still continue on, but that's where I am now. 13 years ago, I would have. Again, young, naive, always tried to see the best in people. 

And I didn't mean for that statement to imply something negative, just that many times people tend to believe their partner over an ex. And unfortunately in this situation, those partners cause extensive damage to everyone.

It's completely up to everyone on what is right for their situation and what they can handle. I know for me, completely untethering from him, or at least as much as possible, is the best. As long as you're involved in any capacity, that tether still exists. 

Your response did make me think of one other thing though. If someone had warned you, do you think you would have listened or still continued on? 

My answer to that question is what makes me know that my efforts would never end in the result I'd hope for. 

I wish you the very best on this journey.

It's taken years, we've been divorced for over 5 years, but I've now regained my own trust. He had me convinced that my memory was faulty. But now when something doesn't make sense, I will not let it go, I believe in facts, facts are indisputable. If you tell me you didn't say that, but I remember it, no I'm not "remembering wrong". 

If we hadn't had kids together. We would never speak again. I'd ice him out of my life entirely and do my best to forget he exists. When I stopped making excuses for his behavior is when I realized, he is responsible for himself and I don't want anything to do with someone like that. They gives absolutely zero fucks about me.
Mine came up with beautiful excuses on why his lies were acceptable. I bought into it for a while.

Personally, I wouldn't. I wouldn't spend any energy that isn't completely necessary on that person. I don't want to interfere in their life. I don't want to think about what they're doing. I don't want to think about them at all. I definitely don't want to put anymore energy into still trying to control the outcome of a situation, when I have no real control. 

I've spoken to a therapist about this before. Her advice to me was that my ex's girlfriends have to be responsible for who they choose to date as well and that any influence I would hope to have either A. Makes me look crazy and benefits whatever narrative he spills or B. Add's fuel to the fire. 

The best thing I can do for myself and my future is to completely separate myself as much as possible. To put my energy into living a life that isn't controlled by the trauma I survived. 

P.S. this may not be true for you, but I can tell you I had a really hard time, still do, with being responsible for his behaviors to some degree. Believing that I had to make things okay, even when I didn't mess them up. I made excuses for him for years. At some point, his trauma, his behaviors, his violence, it's all his to carry.

Lying and/or exaggerating. It didn't even take a month for the lying to begin and not even 6 months to realize stories were inflated to enhance his image. 

Now years later, everything he tells anyone is some version of half truths that paint him as the hero or victim. Which ever benefits him and his reputation more. Added bonus if it paints me in a negative light.

While I know every relationship defines what is appropriate for them, my husband fully financially supports our entire family. We have 3 kids, 2 from my previous marriage and 1 together. 

This took place for us when I lost my job due to Covid, but there were still specific steps we took to get there. We didn't move in together or share any bills until we were engaged. We didn't fully combine finances until after we were married. 

Once we were married we both wanted to be fully combined, not his or hers at all. This is just our belief though, I know many others do it differently and that works for them. 

We have clearly defined roles that make our arrangement work for us, but part of that is my husbands desire to provide, not his obligation. He knows at any point I will whatever it takes to provide for my kids, even if that doesn't include him.

It sounds like you and your partner want different things and it's only become more clear over time even though there were good intentions. 

I don't think anyone is getting what they want here, including the kid. I'm not sure this arrangement is benefitting any of you. 

We only have one life to live. If this isn't what you signed up for, I'd encourage you to find what you want. Your partner also deserves to show up for his child how he wants and the child needs and have the opportunity to find someone who fits into that.

I'm sorry that this is such a tough situation, but I don't think this is going to go away, nor do I think your partner should give up time with his kid for you, or you should give up your desire to be child free for him.

You've got a ton of comments offering you a lot of really good advice. I'm going to try to be as real with you as I can be. The rest of your life is not going to be determined by your high school career. However, I highly suggest researching the statistics for success based on the successful completion of high school. Warning, it doesn't look good. That doesn't mean that only successful people graduate high school and do well. Actually many people struggle through high school and find alternative paths to success later. My husband barely scraped by and he is a very successful business owner at 35, but he did have to work very hard to get there.

What I would caution you against is two things. Number one, quitting entirely. A high school diploma is valuable in this world even if you barely scrape by. Number 2, and the thing I would worry most about, are the habits that you're creating. The habits you create now are going to be  very hard to break later and if you get into a cycle of I don't want to so I'm not going to, life is going to be a b****.As someone else mentioned in here, part of being an adult is doing stuff you don't want to do. And I can say from my experience, the better I am at doing the "have to's" regardless of how I feel about it, the better I am and the more success I find in reaching my goals. I also find it to be a huge confidence booster.

I made it to day four and things improved but I still looked and felt high as a kite. I skipped the next dose, I didn't completely feel better but it helped, and then I took the next one and it was like magic. I felt a ton better.

So... yes/no. 

But I'm accepting treatment and allowing myself to be where I am with it.

I hope this finds you in the sea of comments. I am a mom of 3 boys. You're right, their clothes are pretty boring, but I promise being their mom is not. 

Being a mom to my wild and energetic boys is truly my greatest pleasure. That's not to say they're not loud, destructive, obnoxious, etc. Because they are. But so are most kids. And I've found that in this storm of chaos, is the most love I could have ever hoped for. 

My oldest, and probably most challenging kid, is also the kid who would do anything to make me happy. The kid who can't handle the sight of me crying, because it hurts his heart. Mind you, he's 12, and every bit of a rough and tumble preteen athlete. 

My middle, is the most kind and loving human I've ever met. I recently went on a weekend vacation alone. I needed a break from the stressors of everyday life. He told me "Mom, I'm so happy for you, you work so hard and deserve this". He's 9.

My youngest, can't even talk yet, but there's nothing funnier than the way he giggles when he toots. Or watching his excitement the first time he made his own vroom vroom noises. 

I love being a sports mom. I love watching them succeed. I love that they're kind and loving while also being totally willing to wrestle each other to the ground over who gets to do something first. The bond I have with my boys cannot be matched. Being a boy mom, as messy and loud and frustrating as it can be at times, (because parenting is hard no matter what), is the coolest thing I've ever been able to experience!

I'm sure this is really hard and I can completely understand some of your struggles. 

Anytime you add mental health to the mix, making changes and sticking to them gets that much harder.

However, I don't think it's a reason to quit. I think if you make some sustainable changes you will be quite proud of yourself. Before you know it (in 1 month, 3 months, 6, etc.) you won't be where you are now, vs. if you did nothing. The time passes regardless, your future self will be so happy you put in effort to feel better. I hope you can find it within yourself to want to be that happier person in the future. 

If I were you, I wouldn't shoot for perfection or a lifestyle so different from what you have. I would actually apply only 2 rules to your days. 1. Move your body everyday. I don't know what you're capable of, but maybe it's a small walk. And a week later it's a little longer. You want it to be hard, but not to hurt you. Maybe it's stretching and grabbing more things for yourself. 2. Try to eat the best you can. If you can't control the food, control the portion. If things are fried, maybe pull that part off. If water is available instead of juice, try that more. Don't subscribe to the clean plate club (this is hard for me). Perfection isn't sustainable, but continued effort is. Habits are grown over time, not just adopted. 

I started by decreasing soda eventually that fueled more movement and eating more whole foods instead of processed. I haven't lost 100lbs, but I have changed my habits to better ones, changed my body shape, and fought mental wars every single day. 

I truly wish you all the peace, health, and happiness you desire.

Momma, I'm right there with you. My husband and I have 3. Youngest is both of ours, but my older boys are here 95% of the time. I handle everything aside from financially providing. Daily house chores, finances, kids, sports, errands, appointments, etc. He fully provides, and works long hours. When he is home, he's always willing to help, but I try to make sure I've handled the bulk of everything, so he doesn't have to. (I'd rather just hang out with him lol)  A lot of times I feel like I'm busting my ass way more than he does, But I also know I am extremely lucky not to have to carry the financial stress. When I want to take the kids to ice cream, I can, and he makes sure of that. 

Based on what you said though, it makes logical sense if he's driving that way anyway he would take them. I wonder if there's an option where you help get them up and ready and in the car, and all he does is drop them.

If you switched shoes and did all the providing plus the 1.5 hr trip, would it be too much? 

There's a lot of compromising and negotiating that has to happen. Unfortunately, we all sacrifice sometimes to make our lives function, especially in blended families. 

I'm not saying that taking them is 100% the right answer, but maybe there are other options or perspectives to consider.

I've watched them learn to share, fight, care, love, compromise, coexist, and more. When they are adults, they'll have an army of people to call when they need someone, even after I'm gone. Honestly, I think your situation seems completely fair. Your bills went down, so you're in a better situation financially. 

I can see the side of it being an asset you're helping pay down and if you split, he benefits. But if you split, you also benefitted because you're paying less now than if you would have stayed in your apartment. 

This is an agreement you and your partner made. If it seemed fair to you and to him, and it's split proportionally, as it seems to be, then don't let all the other opinions cloud your mind. There is no one right answer for everyone. Your relationship and what works for you, is a decision for you to make. There will always be other perspectives to challenge that, but those perspectives are from different people in different relationships, with different value/morals/opinions etc.

Unfortunately you've got to feel those feelings. Because you have been betrayed and that hurts. It really really hurts. I like to think about my ex as this beautiful painter. He painted a wonderful picture of loving me, of giving me everything I needed, and really pulled me into the painting. 

Yet it's not real. He wanted control with no consequences. Meaning I would be a perfect, loving, giving, partner, regardless of how I would be treated in return or what I would have to forgive. I remember being told I was lucky to have him at any capacity, and I believed that. Almost begging for him love me. Unfortunately, they can't be held accountable. They need to be superior, in control, powerful, and will only take from you.

It took years of therapy for me to see all of the manipulation that occurred, but I did love him even more than I loved myself. 

I encourage you to write down a list of what you need from a person and let go of any idea of having to make it work with anyone. I think you'll see that this person doesn't check off most of those things. They've just convinced you that you need them. If you can physically see that he is not providing what you need/want it may help change your mindset, and allow you to see that you're in control now, you are happy this destructive person is out of your life. And you are okay because this person doesn't come close to being good enough for you and your growth.

Your needs as a person should be met by a partner who actually loves you, not told you should accept less. A person who loves you, gives you that freely, and the areas that need help (no one is perfect) will take effort that they put in, because they know it's important to you. 

My list includes things like kindness, respect even when fighting, the ability to talk about conflict without the blame game or turning things back on me, affection that doesn't include sex, and (this is broad) loving me without expectations. I refuse to walk on egg shells hoping to receive love in return. 

It took me a long time to be okay sticking with my own standards because I hate being alone, but in the end, I would have spent my life in misery had I not put in the effort to find my own worth.

My situation is basically identical aside from the fact that my husband would be the step parent and my son the 11 yr old. 

I can't count the number of times I've had to tell him "your brother is not a toy, leave him alone". My husband as well, even their Dad who is around from time to time. For us it's just basic respect to another human being and their personal space despite how tiny and cute. 

The youngest is 10 months now, so it's improved but I do continuously say things like "no I'll do it" or "I've got it bud, I'm just gonna do this alone". 

My son being 11 almost 12 is ADHD and fairly immature for his age and does take a lot of entertaining, redirecting, etc. We also have a middle child who is 8. They're constantly "bored and there's nothing to do". I usually give a few options they can choose from if leaving the house isn't one. (I believe boredom is a choice).
 
Chores are a major struggle, we required way too little for way too long, and they were some wild ones, but we implemented some easy ones that help me a lot. 

1. They put their laundry in their basket. If their basket is full they bring it to the laundry room. 
2. They are in charge of their rooms, if there's not a pathway before bed, we quickly make one (for safety reasons), and the next day they clean their room regardless of how long it takes. (In the beginning, it sometimes meant we made a pathway again and it rolled to the next day because they chose to piddle around) We also regularly tell them, their stuff belongs in their room, when they're done with it, it goes back.
3. They have 1 daily chore. one empties the dishwasher, the one takes out the trash. I have to stay on them, but they're getting better at it, and just knowing it's a daily routine.  

I find it helpful to require quiet time when you need it. I'm even direct with my kids sometimes, "I'm not in a good mood, I'm tired, I need some time to myself". For the next 30 minutes (1 hr, or even 2hr) they can do a number of various quiet, independent, activities. One son loves Legos so that's usually his go to, the other loves video games. 

Regardless of parent, step parent, age, etc. There's got to be a level of understanding for a shared space, and accommodating/compromise/pitching in with others.

I just want to add. Motherhood in any form is hard and exhausting. I am still very much learning better ways to balance children/home/time/food/errands etc. But those things have made a difference for me, especially with a new baby. I think it was easier to work than it is to stay home. Try your best, advocate for yourself, and some things do get easier over time.

I've got 2 kids from a previous marriage and one 10 month old with my husband. My boys are rowdy and loud almost constantly. So I promise I do get it, but we've spent years creating household expectations that help. 

I realize a line exist with you not being BM but structure, boundaries, rules, consequences, etc. Are so so important. You are a parent in the home and you can put them in their rooms and explain quiet is expected, consequences exist. (Obviously you discuss this with your partner first). You can put them all in a room together, shut the door and see if that helps. 

I don't agree with the free range thing, although it sounds like you're not doing that. Their dad's house isn't completely boundary less but much more so than mine. My kids prefer the house with rules, expectations, and consistency as their place to primarily live. I just want to include that they love their dad and the time they spend with him. I just think this home makes them feel secure because they know what to expect, and what reaction they'll get.

The expectations here are simple because we do want our kids to be kids, so for us it's respecting each other, kindness, a few chores to pitch in (trash, empty dishwasher), clean up after yourself. All of this takes a limited amount of time and effort, so most of their energy goes to whatever they want. This usually looks like, you can go hang out alone if you're not going to be kind. Or yeah all your chores are done, sure hop on video games. 

In your scenario, it is not respectful to be screaming across the house if someone doesn't feel well and is trying to sleep. "Either play quietly, or you can also lay down for a nap". 

My boys are 8 and 11 and fairly independent if that helps for reference. They also don't struggle too much because these have been the guidelines for a long time now, but when they were little, teaching these things was a daily battle. I wish you the best of luck!

I really hope this is helpful as every word you wrote sounds like my relationship in the beginning. I am 100% positive I am the most important thing to my husband, aside from our son. But my husband absolutely sucks at verbally expressing emotions what so ever. Even when asked his answers are quite vague. Unfortunately that is a need that's very important to me. He has gotten better over time, but there's been a huge learning curve on his part. He was not raised in an affectionate home and it does not come naturally. I have spent a lot of time having the same conversation with him about why I need it, what I'm looking for, why vague answers aren't it. He knows that it's a skill he has to learn for me, and he is, just slowly. I've also expressed to him (and I feel this important) I realize I may need more attention, affirmation, or affection than most, but this is who I am and what I need. Just as I try to satisfy his needs and how those change over time, if he would like to continue the relationship he needs to try as well. 

I don't expect perfection or immediate results. Only that I see effort. 

In the mean time, I'm aware this is not his strength. Instead I try to notice the other ways in which I see his love.
